claim.summary: Trace the final boundary inside Subscriber.invokeSubscriberMethod where the reflective Method.invoke call actually starts, distinguishing outer dispatch and null-check/argument preparation.
details: Subscriber.dispatchEvent schedules a lambda and calls invokeSubscriberMethod(event); this is outside the reflective call boundary.
Subscriber.invokeSubscriberMethod performs the final reflective call through method.invoke(target, checkNotNull(event)).

Java evaluates method-call arguments before entering Method.invoke, so a hook textually before method.invoke(target, checkNotNull(event)) is still before checkNotNull(event) has executed and is too early for this boundary.
Transformation recipe: hoist the checked argument first, e.g. Object checkedEvent = checkNotNull(event); then call the hook; then call method.invoke(target, checkedEvent).
Positive placement pattern: Object checkedEvent = checkNotNull(event); beforeReflectiveSubscriberMethodCall(); method.invoke(target, checkedEvent);
Negative placement pattern: beforeReflectiveSubscriberMethodCall(); method.invoke(target, checkNotNull(event)); because the hook runs before checkNotNull(event) argument preparation.
Hooks before executor.execute, before invokeSubscriberMethod(event), or in Dispatcher/EventBus are also too early.
